messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael had spent two decades trusting his training to read the quiet, methodical language of evidence. That certainty fractured the afternoon the regional logistics hub on the city’s eastern edge ruptured. He had arrived to document compromised structural supports when a secondary detonation tore through the facility. The world did not fade to black; it split into screaming metal and blinding heat. He remembered the sudden, violent shift in air pressure that threw him against a concrete pillar, the deafening collapse of overhead catwalks, and the terrifying, unpredictable rhythm of burning gases swallowing the corridor. He had crawled through smoke and twisted rebar to reach the street, his breath ragged, his hands shaking uncontrollably as sirens finally pierced the chaos. When the smoke cleared, he had walked away, but the ground beneath him felt permanently unstable. In the months that followed, his physiology refused to stand down. Even in his quiet kitchen, his body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, leaving him lying awake with shoulders braced and muscles coiled. A dropped pan or a car backfiring would send his heart hammering, his head snapping toward the noise before he could stop himself. He caught himself jumpy and easily startled during ordinary conversations, certain that his nervous system had broken beyond repair. What frightened him most was the conclusion he kept drawing about himself: his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, particularly the calm, methodical site assessments that had anchored his career. The meticulous patience required to process a scene felt like a foreign language now. Consequently, he stopped driving to new districts. He could no longer tolerate stepping into unfamiliar places because he could not assess the danger, so he began routing his commute through the exact same three streets he had used for years. This avoidance bled directly into his daily work. At the county forensic processing center where he now reviewed only archival case files, the sudden ring of the emergency intercom sent a visceral jolt through his frame. He froze at his stainless-steel workbench, the sterile hum of the equipment warping into the memory of roaring flames. He had withdrawn entirely from field assessments, clinging to the familiar lab to manage the conviction that the world was a dangerous place. His wife noticed the distance hardening around him, how he declined weekend plans to avoid new restaurants or uncharted parking garages. The routine he clung to was fraying. What finally brought Rafael to the clinic was the realization that his avoidance had become a cage. He had missed three major case reviews because he could not bear to leave his known perimeter, and he feared he was losing his professional identity entirely. He sat on the edge of the therapist’s chair, hands clasped tightly, hoping to find a way to quiet the constant readiness in his limbs and to believe, again, that he could navigate a world that no longer felt like a ticking clock.
